analysis.one_liner: Strips local governments of much of their authority to review and regulate cell tower siting.
analysis.headline: The bill has not moved since its September 4, 2025 introduction; it sits in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with zero cosponsors and no votes.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the federal rules governing how states and localities approve cell towers and small wireless antennas. Cities and towns would face strict deadlines to approve or deny each request — as short as 60 days for small facilities on existing structures — and any request they miss the deadline on would be automatically approved. Localities could not discriminate among wireless providers, could not regulate facilities based on radio-frequency emissions if the antennas meet Federal Communications Commission limits, and could only charge fees covering their actual direct costs. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and has not advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Wireless carriers and companies that build and operate cell towers and small-cell installations benefit most. They get faster, more predictable approvals, an automatic approval if a town misses a deadline, clear limits on what local fees can cover, and less ability for communities to block or shape where equipment goes.

how_it_helps.text: States and localities must act on wireless facility requests within set deadlines — 60 to 150 days depending on the request — and a request not acted on in time is deemed granted, without any further action by the government [S2][S3].
Localities may not discriminate among wireless facilities or providers, including by giving exclusive or preferential use of facilities to a particular provider [S2][S3].
Fees localities may charge must be competitively neutral, set in advance, publicly disclosed, and based only on actual and direct costs of review, processing, and repairs [S2][S3].
Localities cannot regulate facility placement based on the environmental effects of radio-frequency emissions if the facility complies with FCC regulations [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: City, county, and town governments pay in lost control and revenue: they lose the ability to use negotiation, timing, or moratoria to shape where towers go, must absorb faster review cycles at fixed staffing, and can only recover actual direct costs. Residents lose local say over where antennas are placed in their neighborhoods.

drawbacks.text: The deemed-granted rule means a town that misses a 60- or 90-day deadline — whether from understaffing, a backlog, or an oversight — automatically approves the tower, with no local vote or hearing at all [S2][S3].

Localities are barred from considering the environmental effects of radio-frequency emissions for FCC-compliant facilities, removing one of the few health-related questions communities can raise, though FCC limits already govern emissions nationally [S2][S3].
Fees must be limited to actual and direct costs, which cuts fee revenue many small localities use to cover the full cost of administering permits and right-of-way upkeep [S2][S3].

The bill does preserve some local authority: objective engineering standards, safety requirements, aesthetic and concealment rules, and a 30-day window to flag incomplete applications remain allowed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Faster tower approvals can mean quicker coverage improvements and fewer dead zones, which matters to consumers and to public-safety communications. But the bill goes well beyond speed: it converts missed deadlines into automatic approvals, blocks local review of radio-frequency effects, and caps fees at bare cost recovery. The balance tilts toward the carriers' convenience and away from community control, and it does so with no offsetting public benefit such as a coverage obligation, rural build-out requirement, or consumer-price provision.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 4, 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no votes, and no cosponsors [S1][S5][S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Latta (R-OH) introduced the bill in the House on September 4, 2025 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
No further action has been taken since the referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost much of anything; the bill is dormant. If it stays dormant, local governments and neighborhood residents keep their current authority over tower siting.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Latta
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor; it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, on which he sits

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only a single Republican sponsor with no cosponsors, no votes, and no recorded opposition, so no partisan or interest-group split is visible yet.

industries.note: The bill gives carriers fast, automatic approvals for towers and small cells, prohibits local discrimination among providers, and caps local fees at actual direct costs — cutting the time, money, and negotiation that carriers spend on permitting. The public gets faster deployment in principle, but loses local say over placement and pays through reduced municipal control.

Companies that build, own, and lease wireless infrastructure get shorter approval cycles and automatic approval on missed deadlines, letting them place more equipment faster. Better coverage could reach customers, but the gain flows through private infrastructure firms rather than to any public build-out obligation.

Localities lose the practical tools of zoning leverage: strict shot clocks with deemed-granted results, no tolling during moratoria, fee caps at actual direct costs, and a bar on considering radio-frequency environmental effects. Their fiscal interest in permit revenue and their constituents' interest in local control both take the hit.

analysis.trajectory: With one sponsor, no cosponsors, and no committee activity two months after introduction, the realistic path is that the bill stays in committee unless telecom preemption gains a hearing in this Congress. Versions of these siting preemption rules have been adopted by FCC order before, so carriers may pursue that route instead; a bill like this passing into law without broader sponsorship is unlikely.
